name: Furnas suture otoplasty

card.summary: A cartilage-sparing ear-pinning surgery that uses sutures between the ear's concha and the mastoid bone to set back prominent ears so they sit closer to the head.
card.note: Surgical procedure; complications include suture extrusion, hematoma and recurrence.

quick.overview:
Furnas suture otoplasty is an ear-pinning technique described by D. Furnas in 1968. Surgeons place stitches joining the conchal bowl of the ear to the mastoid bone behind it, which reduces the angle between ear and head and brings protruding ears closer in.

The appearance payoff is ears that sit flatter against the head, which is the usual aim for people bothered by prominent ears. Clinical series report high satisfaction, and the technique is commonly paired with the Mustardé method, which creates the ear's antihelical fold.
quick.how: The operation is performed by a plastic or ENT surgeon, usually as an outpatient procedure under local or general anesthesia. A dressing is worn for several days and then a snug headband, typically for several weeks. Surgeons often combine concha-mastoid sutures with other steps depending on which part of the ear projects.
quick.risks: Reported complications include suture extrusion (the most common), hematoma, infection, recurrence of the prominence needing revision, asymmetry and overcorrection. Series report these as low-frequency; a surgeon consult determines suitability.

lead: Furnas suture otoplasty is a surgical technique for correcting prominent ears using concha-mastoid sutures, which draw the conchal bowl toward the mastoid and reduce the conchomastoid angle. It was described by D. Furnas in 1968 [1].

People seek it to have ears that lie closer to the head. It is a cartilage-sparing, suture-based approach, in the same group as the Mustardé technique (described in 1963), and the two are often combined [1][2].
Published series, mostly retrospective, report low complication rates and high satisfaction. Variations such as barbed absorbable sutures have been compared against classic knotted sutures [3].

chain: Ears sit closer to the head
angle.text: The procedure sets back protruding ears so they lie flatter against the head. Patients choose it to change ear prominence.

paras: Wikipedia's otoplasty article classes the Furnas and Mustardé methods as Group I techniques that keep cartilage intact and reshape the ear with sutures. Furnas' concha-mastoid sutures reduce the angle between concha and mastoid, and are sometimes paired with conchal excision [1].
Patients commonly wear a loose dressing for several days, then a snug headband while sleeping for roughly three to six weeks. Bruising and swelling usually settle within about two weeks [1].

A comparative study of 25 patients operated with the Furnas technique and 23 with a knotless barbed absorbable suture variant found low complication rates in both. The classic-suture group needed reoperation in five cases for recurrence and one for asymmetry, and four had sutures removed for pain or extrusion, while the barbed group needed none. Satisfaction was 91.6% versus 95.7% [3].

A retrospective study of 172 patients (343 procedures) using combined Mustardé-Furnas surgery found 77.9% met all six McDowell and Wright success criteria at 12 months, and satisfaction rose as more criteria were met [4]. A 200-patient series using a modified Mustardé-Furnas cartilage-sparing method reported hematoma in two patients, suture extrusion as the most common complication, and recurrence needing surgery in eight [5].

Another comparison of 78 patients found differing results between a standard Mustardé-Furnas approach and one with added antihelix-mastoid sutures [2], and a 100-patient follow-up compared suture materials combined with a Furnas conchal setback [6].

Suture extrusion is described as the most common complication, sometimes with painful granulomas, and overcorrection is considered the most significant complication since it can create an unnatural contour. Hematoma needs prompt drainage and infection is treated aggressively to avoid chondritis [1][5].
